transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Torres (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Aurora CTO), Sofia Martinez (Aurora ML Platform Lead), Omar Haddad (Aurora SRE)

Summary (auto):
High-level technical deep dive focused on GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs usage, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, and quantization effects. Agreed next steps to run scripted microbenchmarks and schedule an on-prem pilot.

Topics: kernel selection; TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM; CUDA graphs; KV cache / prefix caching; batch sizing; quantization profiles; VPC/on-prem considerations.

-- Transcript --
[00:00:00] Jamie: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off in a minute. this is Jamie from Redwood, with Priya our infra SE.
[00:00:12] Priya: hi all, ok quick agenda, we wanna walk through profiling results, show kernel selection behavior, then do Q&A and plan a pilot. sound good?
[00:00:25] Liam: yep sounds good. we most interested in latency SLOs at p95 and cost per token tradeoffs, and on-prem constraints re: VPC.
[00:00:35] Sofia: and we have a pretty bursty workload — lots of short chat prompts, some long generation for summaries.
[00:00:44] Omar: i'll be listening for network/VPC setup and any firewall ports needed for the private control plane.
[00:00:52] Priya: cool. quick context from us: we profiled a few models on A100 and H100 hardware. we ran vLLM (we sometimes say v-llm) and our TensorRT-LLM path. note: transcripts may call it 't r t llm' in notes, ha.
[00:01:05] Priya: objective is to compare kernel selection, cudda graphs (cudda vs cuda), and how KV cache warm vs cold affects latency.
[00:01:18] Jamie: ok i'll drop the high level numbers first then Priya will dig into traces. baseline: with vLLM we saw p50 ~18ms/token, p95 ~42ms/token on H100 for 2048 context at batch=1. TensorRT-LLM path was p50 ~14ms/token, p95 ~31ms/token for same config before quantization.
[00:01:40] Liam: those are promising, can you explain why tensorrt is lower at p95?
[00:01:46] Priya: yeah so two things: kernel fusion and half-precision kernels that are tuned for cublas/cudnn replacements; plus cudagraphs reduce launch overhead for autoreg loops. also our kernel selector will pick different matmul/attention kernels based on sequence length and head dims.
[00:02:05] Sofia: when you say kernel selector, is that dynamic per-request or static per-deploy?
[00:02:11] Priya: good q. it's heuristic-driven at load time, with a runtime fallback. we profile micro-batches at start and pick the fastest kernels for the expected seqlen dist. for outliers we have a fallback to a more generic kernel which slightly increases latency.
[00:02:29] [00:02:30] Omar: is that selector open to override? we might want to pin kernels for regression testing.
[00:02:37] Priya: yes you can pin kernels in the deploy config or set a forced mode to avoid dynamic switching — useful for deterministic perf.
[00:02:46] Jamie: ok Priya, show the trace for the 512->2048 prefix scenario.
[00:02:52] Priya: sure, pulling up the flamegraph — so here at [00:03:00] you can see attention kernels dominate for long seqs, but for shorter seq we get better utilization via fused matmul. also note the KV cache lookups add about 6-8ms when cold — that's overhead on first request.
[00:03:18] Liam: that KV overhead concerns us because we do multi-turn chat; cold starts will hurt user experience. any mitigations?
[00:03:25] Priya: yes — automatic prefix/KV caching: we can warm the cache with a prefetch step or keep hot contexts resident using TTL. also batching small concurrent requests reduces per-token overhead because amortized kernel launch cost drops.
[00:03:42] Sofia: about batching — our workload is many users single-turn but high concurrency. how do you balance latency vs throughput?
[00:03:49] Priya: we use a hybrid scheduler: strict latency buckets for p99-sensitive routes and opportunistic batching for everything else. you can set per-route SLOs in the config.
[00:03:59] [00:04:05] Jamie: quick interjection — cost tradeoffs: larger batch sizes cut cost per token but raise tail latency; quantization helps both but can degrade quality on some models.
[00:04:16] Liam: we care about hallucination rates for summaries — quantization sounds risky. what levels do you support?
[00:04:22] Priya: we support int8, and 4-bit FP variants with calibration. our recommendation path includes model-specific quant profiles; we run evals on prompt sets to check quality regressions. we'll share the quant recommendation report.
[00:04:36] Sofia: have you seen any models where int8 breaks summaries?
[00:04:40] Priya: yes, some Llama-family variants show small regression at aggressive 4-bit settings. that's why we pair quant with eval thresholds; if quality regresses we fall back to int16 or mixed precision.
[00:04:52] [00:05:00] Jamie: Priya, can you talk about CUDA graphs in more detail and when they help?
[00:05:06] Priya: sure — cudagraphs (we sometimes call them c u d a-graphs) reduce per-iteration launch costs by capturing the computation graph for a fixed control flow. they shine when you have stable sequence lengths and batch sizes. for highly dynamic seqlen patterns they give less benefit because you'd need to maintain many graphs.
[00:05:24] Omar: any memory overhead for multiple graphs?
[00:05:27] Priya: yes, each graph holds state and some kernel buffers; we cap the number of cached graphs and evict LRU. memory overhead is modest relative to model KV size but it's a factor on memory-constrained nodes.
[00:05:40] Liam: what about multi-GPU scaling? we are interested in both single large GPU latency and multi-GPU throughput.
[00:05:48] Priya: for multi-GPU we use tensor parallel kernels (tpp) and/or model sharding. kernel selection changes: some kernels are better for single-GPU fused ops, others are optimized for NCCL-backed allreduce patterns. tensorrt-llm path currently focuses on single-node multi-instance execution; we have strategies for pipeline + tensor parallelism but that increases complexity.
[00:06:08] [00:06:15] Sofia: can you quantify the tradeoff — assume 4x H100, what's throughput gain vs single node?
[00:06:20] Priya: ballpark depends on model and batch shapes; with efficient tensor parallel kernels we saw ~3.3x throughput for a 4x H100 config on one of our tests due to comm overheads. we'll include the exact runs in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[00:06:33] Liam: ok thanks. switching gears: vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM — what are the error modes or edge cases?
[00:06:41] Priya: vLLM is great for low-latency, small-batch scenarios because of its scheduler and KV cache handling; TensorRT-LLM excels when kernels can be fused and graph captured. vLLM sometimes wins on irregular prompt patterns. tensorrt wins on steady-state high-throughput. also tensorrt path is more sensitive to model ops that aren't supported by TRT, where we fallback to CPU or custom kernels.
[00:07:03] [00:07:15] Jamie: example: if a model uses rotary embeddings vs ALiBi — kernel availability can differ and cause slower fallback?
[00:07:20] Priya: correct. we maintain a compatibility matrix. if a required op lacks a TRT kernel we either plug in a custom CUDA kernel or run that op in a slower path.
[00:07:31] Omar: are custom kernels sandboxed for security? we run in a regulated environment.
[00:07:36] Priya: yes, in Private mode custom kernels are built into the customer's runtime image and go through our build+sign process. we can discuss HSM/KMS and code signing in the security call.
[00:07:47] [00:08:00] Liam: networking — for private deployments what does control-plane vs data-plane look like? we can't have egress to the public internet.
[00:08:07] Jamie: for Redwood Private the control plane can be a private control plane option or a customer-managed control plane — we support VPC peering, private endpoints, and an on-prem package that avoids any outbound call. we will share the VPC network diagram and firewall ports.
[00:08:24] Sofia: nice. what about data residency / audit logs?
[00:08:27] Jamie: we provide audit logs, per-request metadata, and optional log forwarding to your SIEM. SOC2 summary and compliance docs will be included in the follow-up packet.
[00:08:37] [00:08:45] Priya: back to perf, here's a gotcha: quantization sometimes changes the numerical stability of attention kernels, which can cause divergence on long generations. we track this in our eval harness and flag regressions.
[00:09:00] Liam: do you have an automated regression hook so we can gate rollouts?
[00:09:05] Priya: yes, Redwood Optimize includes eval gating — you can provide your prompt set and acceptance thresholds. rollouts can be canaryed and automatically rolled back on regressions.
[00:09:17] [00:09:30] Sofia: you mentioned KV cache warm vs cold earlier. can you walk through a concrete example with numbers?
[00:09:36] Priya: sure. example: 2048 context, first token generation (cold) includes cache population and is ~40-55ms extra per request; subsequent tokens drop to the p50 cited earlier. with prefix warm we often cut 1st-token overhead by ~70%.
[00:09:56] Omar: how long do you keep hot contexts? TTL?
[00:10:00] Priya: TTL configurable per-route; default 15 minutes but you can tweak. also cache eviction is LRU-based; if memory pressure is high we evict larger contexts first.
[00:10:13] [00:10:30] Jamie: question from the notes — how stable are the cudagraphs across driver updates and CUDA versions?
[00:10:36] Priya: cudagraphs depend on driver/runtime ABI; we test across supported CUDA versions and have a compatibility matrix. major driver upgrades can require re-capture of graphs; we advise scheduled maintenance windows.
[00:10:50] Liam: do you provide tooling to re-capture graphs automatically on upgrade?
[00:10:55] Priya: yes, we have a capture daemon that can re-warm graphs during a controlled window. it's part of our upgrade playbook.
[00:11:05] [00:11:15] Sofia: any real-world numbers on cost delta vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM for our workload?
[00:11:20] Jamie: depends on SLOs but typical numbers from our runs: TensorRT path 20-40% lower $/token at high throughput; vLLM can be cheaper for low QPS low-batch patterns. we'll run your sample to get exact numbers.
[00:11:36] Omar: curious about monitoring — what traces/metrics do you expose for kernel-level perf?
[00:11:41] Priya: we emit per-kernel timing, GPU util, kernel selection events, KV cache hit/miss, per-route SLOs, and token-level traces. you can integrate with Prometheus/Grafana or our Console.
[00:11:56] [00:12:10] Jamie: demo time — Priya, walk us through a short trace capture.
[00:12:14] Priya: pulling up a trace... so at 00:12:30 you see a capture of a 512 token generation. note the cudagraph capture phase at sequence start, then steady token gen where launch overhead is minimal. at 00:12:55 you can see the fallback kernel path for an edge op.
[00:12:58] Liam: that fallback spike is concerning; is there a way to pre-detect and avoid it?
[00:13:03] Priya: yes we have an offline compatibility scan to detect unsupported ops and warn; you can pin a deployment to avoid automatic fallback, or provide a custom kernel.
[00:13:12] [00:13:30] Sofia: about custom kernels — what's the dev workflow? we have internal ML ops that write CUDA kernels.
[00:13:36] Priya: we provide a kernel SDK and build pipeline; kernels are signed and tested in a sandbox before being allowed into the Private runtime. we can run a joint integration with your kernel team.
[00:13:48] Omar: does that require root on nodes? not ideal.
[00:13:52] Priya: no — the build happens in CI and artifacts are deployed via our package manager; you don't need to give node root.
[00:14:00] [00:14:15] Jamie: ok quick poll — are there any blockers on your side to start the pilot?
[00:14:21] Liam: we need to confirm security review and access to an H100 test node for on-prem.
[00:14:27] Sofia: plus we need the benchmarking spreadsheet and instructions.
[00:14:31] Jamie: we'll send that today.
[00:14:35] [00:14:45] Priya: one more thing: when you run the microbenchmarks please include cold vs warm KV runs, varied batch sizes 1,4,8,16, and a mix of short and long seqs. that helps our kernel selector tuning.
[00:14:58] Liam: noted.
[00:15:05] [00:15:30] -- Mid-call technical deep dive --
[00:15:30] Priya: pulling up kernel selection heuristics: we consider seqlen, head size, and model-specific op mix. for attention we choose between split-attention kernels vs fused attention+softmax. fused reduces memory traffic but is less flexible.
[00:15:51] Sofia: are these heuristics ML-driven or rule-based?
[00:15:55] Priya: hybrid — rules seeded by offline profiling and then refined by online telemetry. we avoid fully opaque ML decisions in production runs to keep determinism.
[00:16:07] Liam: can we get those heuristics exported for audit?
[00:16:11] Priya: yes we can share the rules and thresholds — we'll include it in the tech appendix.
[00:16:20] [00:16:45] Jamie: question about memory layout — do you use a custom memory allocator?
[00:16:50] Priya: we use a custom GPU allocator tuned for KV caches and per-request scratch. avoids fragmentation and helps with multi-tenant scenarios. memory pooling also reduces allocations during capture.
[00:17:05] Omar: fragmentation has bitten us before. will your allocator show memory pressure metrics?
[00:17:10] Priya: yes, per-node GPU memory used, fragmentation ratio, and eviction counts are exposed.
[00:17:18] [00:17:30] Sofia: how do you handle model updates/rollouts for kernel compatibility?
[00:17:35] Priya: rollouts run canary profiles and a capture + eval window; if kernel mismatches are detected we halt the rollout. you can also pin model versions to prevent automatic optimizer changes.
[00:17:50] [00:18:00] Liam: regulatory question — for Private deployments can we keep keys in our HSM?
[00:18:05] Jamie: yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support envelope encryption; key material stays on your side.
[00:18:12] Omar: logs — can we forward raw request traces to our SIEM?
[00:18:16] Jamie: yes, and you can control PII redaction rules.
[00:18:24] [00:18:40] Priya: quick note: sometimes perf spreadsheets show surprising outliers due to power/clock management on GPUs; make sure power profiles and MIG settings are consistent across runs.
[00:18:51] Liam: good call. we'll standardize node images and power settings.
[00:18:56] [00:19:10] -- Later in call: concrete pilot planning --
[00:19:10] Jamie: proposed pilot: two-week profiling run, one H100 node in your lab or our Dedicated node, run microbenchmarks + production trace replay, and then a joint postmortem.
[00:19:24] Sofia: two weeks seems fine. can we tighten to one week for initial numbers?
[00:19:29] Jamie: we can do an initial one-week run focused on p50/p95, then extend as needed.
[00:19:35] Omar: what data do you need from us?
[00:19:38] Jamie: sample model, 10M token prompt set (anonymized), production traffic replay or representative traces, and access to a test node or permission for Redwood to run on Dedicated.
[00:19:51] Sofia: we'll prepare the sample set and try to scrub PII.
[00:19:55] [00:20:10] Priya: also include your target SLOs and cost targets so we can recommend quant/batch profiles.
[00:20:17] Liam: our target p95 < 80ms for chat, and cost target about 30% lower than current internal infra.
[00:20:24] Jamie: noted.
[00:20:30] [00:20:45] -- Q&A and wrap-up --
[00:20:45] Sofia: small nit — in the trace you mentioned fallback to CPU for some ops; does that happen in the hot path?
[00:20:52] Priya: only if the op is unsupported and no custom kernel provided; it's rare but detectable. we try to avoid CPU fallback for p95 critical routes.
[00:21:02] Omar: what's the expected turnaround to add a custom kernel if we need one?
[00:21:06] Priya: depending on complexity 2-4 weeks for testing and signing, faster for small ops.
[00:21:14] Liam: ok will prioritize that in the pilot if needed.
[00:21:20] [00:21:30] Jamie: recap of next steps: we'll send benchmark spreadsheet (today), schedule pilot week of 10/27, Priya to run microbenchmarks and run initial TensorRT vs vLLM comparisons, Aurora to provide sample model and traces.
[00:21:46] Sofia: yep. also can you share a sample config for pinning kernels and TTL settings?
[00:21:52] Priya: will include sample deploy config and capture flags.
[00:21:57] Liam: perfect. thanks everyone.
[00:22:05] Jamie: thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links to docs: benchmark sheet (https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/aurora-template), cudagraphs guide (https://redwood.ai/docs/cuda-graphs), security pack (https://redwood.ai/security/soc2-summary.pdf).
[00:22:20] Sofia: got it.
[00:22:25] Omar: thanks.
[00:22:30] -- End of call (approx 62 minutes total)
